sources.title: Human History Map research coverage registry

sources.title: Human History Map 2000 BCE borders
sources.note: Control snapshot before the exact target appears and decoded regional point owners.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 BCE borders
sources.note: First exact Polygon, full coordinate audit, bounds, membership and adjacent owners.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 CE borders
sources.note: One of nine distinct geometry hashes despite unchanged tested point membership.

sources.title: Human History Map 1279 CE borders
sources.note: Small coordinate change defining a distinct exact geometry shared with 1300.

sources.title: Human History Map 1400 CE borders
sources.note: Last pre-1492 target interval and geometry later repeated at 1500.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 CE borders
sources.note: Exact target absence and replacement by many named overlapping Indigenous atlas layers.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 CE borders
sources.note: Post-contact exact Polygon with a further coordinate hash and stable sampled membership.

sources.title: Human History Map 1650 CE borders
sources.note: First visibly clipped Polygon as colonial atlas ownership reaches several sampled edges.

sources.title: Human History Map 1715 CE borders
sources.note: Only exact MultiPolygon, with two audited components and a separate Uruguay fragment.

sources.title: Human History Map 1783 CE borders
sources.note: Major shrink to a northern Patagonian coastal Polygon repeated through 1815.

sources.title: Human History Map 1878 CE borders
sources.note: Final exact interval, northward expansion, geometry hash and national-state seams.

sources.title: Human History Map 1880 CE borders
sources.note: Endpoint control where Argentina and neighboring states replace the exact target.

sources.title: Politis and Borrero, The Archaeology of the Pampas and Patagonia
sources.note: Regional archaeological synthesis emphasizing environmental, technological and social variation over deep time.

sources.title: Borrero and colleagues, opportunistic animal resources in Pampa and Patagonia
sources.note: Cut-marked guanaco assemblages and ephemeral sites reveal localized use of bogged or recently dead animals.

sources.title: Gordón and colleagues, wild plants and exotic maize in pre-Hispanic Patagonia
sources.note: Stable-isotope models and direct dates quantify terrestrial animals, wild plants, fish and limited imported maize.

sources.title: Postillone and colleagues, ancient mitochondrial genomes from the Argentinian Pampas
sources.note: Eighteen ancient mitochondrial genomes show regional history while illustrating genetic sampling and identity limits.

sources.title: Serna and colleagues, mobility and interaction networks in northern Patagonia
sources.note: Strontium isotopes and exotic items distinguish mostly local residence from a few exceptional journeys.

sources.title: CONICET, multifunctional pots from central Patagonia
sources.note: Institutional report on local clays, vessel residues and mixed plant, terrestrial and marine foods.

sources.title: Musaubach and Berón, plant residues in western Pampas pottery
sources.note: Pot residues contain grass, Prosopis and maize microremains in a water-limited residential setting.

sources.title: Alcaráz, subsistence and ritual in the eastern Pampa-Patagonia transition
sources.note: Zooarchaeology at Zoko Andi shows broad-spectrum strategies, recurring occupation and local landscape building.

sources.title: Messineo and colleagues, Holocene occupations at Laguna de los Pampas
sources.note: Excavated dune-field locality connects water, recurrent occupation, stone technology and wider Pampean interaction.

sources.title: Scheifler and colleagues, mobility and territories in central Argentine dunefields
sources.note: Stone sourcing shows contacts across territories rather than one endlessly roaming undifferentiated population.

sources.title: Agnolin and colleagues, bolas and hunting technology in southern Patagonia
sources.note: Chronology and raw materials track bolas, projectile points, drought and changing logistical mobility.

sources.title: Di Prado and colleagues, pottery at Laguna Las Lágrimas
sources.note: Pampean hunter-gatherer pottery study localizes clay choices, manufacture and vessel variability.

sources.title: Suárez and colleagues, recurrent occupation in Uruguayan shelters and mounds
sources.note: Stratigraphy and radiocarbon dates show repeated shelter use, mound links and later Guaraní contact.

sources.title: Colonese and colleagues, fish feasting in Cerritos pottery
sources.note: Lipid and isotope evidence distinguishes fish cooking, plant processing and possible fermented drinks.

sources.title: Gazzán and colleagues, mounds to villages in Uruguay
sources.note: Remote sensing and excavation reveal multifunctional earthen mounds, settlements, routes and wetland engineering.

sources.title: Bonomo, Politis and Gianotti, Paraná Delta mounds and horticulture
sources.note: Critical review of mound building, lowland settlement, horticulture and possible inequality in the Paraná Delta.

sources.title: Loponte and colleagues, mortuary pottery in the Paraná Basin
sources.note: Microscopy, chemistry and residues test a mortuary interpretation for unusual tubular ceramic artifacts.

sources.title: Cornero and colleagues, microstructures and archaeobotany in the middle Paraná floodplain
sources.note: Dental calculus, burial sediment and vessel residues identify maize, beans and squash beside fishing and hunting.

sources.title: Gianotti and colleagues, orientations of Indigenous mounds in Uruguay
sources.note: First archaeoastronomical tests examine mound orientation while carefully separating alignments from demonstrated beliefs.

sources.title: Berón, Aranda and Luna, children as social actors at Chenque I
sources.note: Subadult burials document childhood mortality, mortuary treatment and interpersonal violence in western Pampas.

sources.title: Politis, archaeology of childhood in the Pampas
sources.note: Ethnoarchaeological comparison develops cautious expectations for recognizing children making and using objects.

sources.title: Ramos van Raap and colleagues, childhood in Lower Paraná wetlands
sources.note: Bioarchaeological study links child lives and deaths to abundant low-risk wetland resources without universalizing roles.

sources.title: García Guraieb, paleopathology in southern Patagonia
sources.note: Regional review evaluates stress, disease, parasites and contact-era change in hunter-gatherer skeletal evidence.

sources.title: Fugassa and colleagues, Late Holocene parasites in Patagonian coprolites
sources.note: Microscopy finds parasite eggs while warning that some coprolites may be human or carnivore.

sources.title: Estomba, Ladio and Lozada, medicinal plant knowledge in northwestern Patagonia
sources.note: Modern family interviews document localized Mapuche medicinal knowledge as a labeled later comparison.

sources.title: Steibel, plant names and uses among Ranquel people
sources.note: Historical and modern interviews record Ranquel plant knowledge, language loss and continued rural practice.

sources.title: Museo Roca, Indigenous dwellings and their changes
sources.note: Museum synthesis of historical hide tents, seasonal settlements, household work and source limitations.

sources.title: Museo Histórico Nacional, a Ranquel poncho with a documented history
sources.note: Object biography ties weaving, women artisans, diplomacy, identity and a named nineteenth-century Ranquel household.

sources.title: Ortelli, Indigenous societies of the Pampas in the colonial period
sources.note: Historical synthesis replaces migration stereotypes with local adaptation, exchange, diplomacy and conflict.

sources.title: Taylor and colleagues, early domestic horse use in southern Patagonia
sources.note: Direct radiocarbon, zooarchaeology and biomolecular evidence traces Indigenous horse use and dispersal.

sources.title: Nuevo Delaunay and colleagues, glass and stoneware tools in southern Patagonia
sources.note: Archaeology and documents show creative reuse, hide work and uneven colonial impacts among named regions.

sources.title: Giordano, Indigenous writing and bureaucracy in the toldos
sources.note: Nineteenth-century Spanish correspondence shows Indigenous diplomatic literacy mediated by named authors and scribes.

sources.title: Museo Roca, the long Pampean-Patagonian frontier
sources.note: Museum account emphasizes trade, diplomacy and conflict before late nineteenth-century state campaigns.

sources.title: Museo Roca, emergence of Argentina national territories
sources.note: Institutional history dates congressionally authorized campaigns from 1878 to 1885 and explains state expansion.

sources.title: Pérez, Conquest of the Desert and genocide studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed historiography analyzes war, assimilation and genocide frameworks for Mapuche-Tehuelche North Patagonia.

sources.title: Nagy and Papazian, military camps and Indigenous confinement
sources.note: Historical archaeology documents attacks, capture, forced movement, family separation and coerced labor.

sources.title: Argentina INAI, map of Indigenous peoples and communities
sources.note: Official registers map living Mapuche, Tehuelche, Ranquel and other communities without erasing self-identification.

sources.title: Chile Council of National Monuments, Patagonian rock art
sources.note: Institutional overview localizes hand stencils, guanaco scenes and geometric designs across Patagonian sites.

sources.title: CONICET, Guanacos of the steppe exhibition
sources.note: Research-based museum exhibition traces guanaco meat, fat, sinew, hide, tools and shelters.

sources.title: Vecchi, documentary evidence for boleadoras in Pampa and Patagonia
sources.note: Archaeology, historical sources and experiments distinguish weapon types, hunting tactics and manufacture.

sources.title: Riede and colleagues, hunter-gatherer children object play and tool use
sources.note: Cross-cultural review supports play and peer learning as comparison, not a local prehistoric script.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Changing atlas umbrella across Pampas, Uruguay and northern to central Patagonia, circa 1500 BCE to 1880 CE.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id and display label are preserved as atlas metadata, not an ancient or modern self-name.
Thirty-five exact features form nine geometry signatures plus controls before, during the 1492 gap and after 1880.
Early geometry includes Uruguay and parts of Patagonia while excluding sampled Buenos Aires, Mendoza, Bariloche and far southern Patagonia.
The target is not one people, language, ancestry, economy, archaeological culture, religion or polity.
Named archaeological sites, Indigenous peoples and historical communities remain localized and chronologically controlled.
Direct finds, scientific inference, historical documentation and later ethnographic comparison are explicitly separated.
No written sample is supplied because no single text can represent the exact umbrella across its footprint and interval.
The 1880 endpoint records state expansion and an atlas redraw, not a shared cultural fall or extinction.
